subject: feminism
title: The Modern Women's Foundation (現代婦女基金會): Taiwan's first women's protection center and the laws it built
dek: Founded in 1987 by Pan Wei-kang, a local councillor who later became a long-serving legislator, Modern Women's Foundation became Taiwan's first organization dedicated to protecting women from sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment when those crimes had no legal framework and police would not take reports. It drafted or co-drafted four major laws between 1997 and 2005, including Asia's first domestic violence prevention act, and continues to serve more than 8,000 victims each year. This lesson explains what a protection center does, how it differs from an advocacy organization, how Taiwan's charity transparency laws work, and what a vintage shop partnership could mean.
era: 1987 to the present: founding in May 1987, about two and a half months before martial law was lifted in July, the 1988 Women's Guardian Center, the law-drafting campaigns of the 1990s after Deng Ru-wen's case and Peng Wan-ru's murder, the 2001 national 113 hotline, court service centers and professional services after 2002, and today's work against dating violence and stalking
honesty: This lesson is text only. The history and service figures come from Modern Women's Foundation's own English and Chinese pages (About us, 認識現代, 年度大事紀, 財務簽證報告). Dates of Deng Ru-wen's sentencing and parole come from the Chinese Wikipedia article and the press reports it cites; Pan Wei-kang's career comes from English Wikipedia and the foundation's own biography; Peng Wan-ru details come from English Wikipedia. The early drafting history of the domestic violence bill, the NT$1 million research grant and the 1996 night march come from a 2022 Taipei Times 'Taiwan in Time' article. Sources disagree on Deng Ru-wen's age when Lin A-chi first raped her, so the lesson does not give a number. Legal obligations were checked against the Foundations Act text on the Ministry of Justice law database. The 8,000-victims and 3,000-families figures are the foundation's own claims. I did not read the scanned audited financial statements line by line, so the lesson gives no income or spending figures. I removed several details I could not confirm, including an award claim, a claim about which courts the foundation ran service centres in by 2013, and an unsupported claim that the foundation published combined financial reports until 2015. This is a study guide, not legal or partnership advice: before cool dairy signs anything, confirm details with the organization and, if needed, an accountant or lawyer.

timeline.label: Foundation established
timeline.detail: Pan Wei-kang, then a member of the Taipei City Council, and a group of advocates establish Modern Women's Foundation on 1 May 1987, about two and a half months before martial law was lifted on 15 July. The original mission is to help women balance traditional and modern roles.

timeline.label: Women's Guardian Center
timeline.detail: Realizing that women lack even basic safety protections, the foundation opens Taiwan's first Women's Guardian Center (婦女護衛中心), offering legal, medical and police-accompaniment services to victims of sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment.

timeline.label: Deng Ru-wen case
timeline.detail: In October 1993, Deng Ru-wen kills her abusive husband after years of violence. Her case exposes the absence of domestic violence laws and galvanizes women's groups, including Modern Women's Foundation, to draft legislation.

timeline.label: Peng Wan-ru murdered; drafting resumes
timeline.detail: DPP Women's Affairs Department director Peng Wan-ru is raped and murdered in Kaohsiung on 30 November 1996. Her death reignites public outrage over women's safety. The same year Modern Women's Foundation sets up a drafting committee for a domestic violence law, with judge Kao Feng-hsian as the drafter, and its sexual assault bill gains momentum.

timeline.label: Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Taiwan enacts the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act on 22 January 1997, establishing prevention centers, victim services, offender treatment and a national registry. Modern Women's Foundation had commissioned Liao Shu-wen to draft the bill, and women legislators from the KMT, DPP and New Party pushed it through together.

timeline.label: Domestic Violence Prevention Act
timeline.detail: On 24 June 1998, Taiwan becomes Asia's first country to enact a domestic violence prevention law with a civil protection order system. The bill came from Modern Women's Foundation's drafting committee, with judge Kao Feng-hsian as drafter. The protection order provisions take effect in June 1999.

timeline.label: Criminal Code amendment
timeline.detail: Legislator Pan Wei-kang leads the amendment of Criminal Code Chapter 16, which moves sexual assault crimes from 'offenses against morality' to a new chapter on 'offenses against sexual autonomy,' changing the legal frame from public decency to personal rights and making marital rape a crime.

timeline.label: 113 protection hotline established
timeline.detail: On 13 January 2001, the Ministry of the Interior consolidates earlier hotlines into the 113 protection hotline, a 24-hour national service for domestic violence, sexual assault and child protection. It is run by the government, not by Modern Women's Foundation.

timeline.label: Court service centers
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation establishes Taiwan's first family-violence service center inside Shilin District Court, with social workers helping victims file protection orders, access legal advice and connect to welfare resources. The model spreads nationwide.

timeline.label: Sexual Harassment Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation proposes a Sexual Harassment Prevention Act to cover harassment in public spaces not addressed by workplace or school laws. The act is promulgated on 5 February 2005 and takes effect one year later, on 5 February 2006.

timeline.label: Sexual assault law reform
timeline.detail: A drafting team led by foundation board member and lawyer Lai Fang-yu, with former executive director Lin Mei-hsun, lawyer Wang Ju-hsuan, professors Wang Pei-ling and Lu Ying-chieh and Liao Shu-wen, pushes amendments to the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act protecting child victims' court rights, establishing expert witnesses and banning unauthorized sharing of victim information.

timeline.label: Trauma recovery center
timeline.detail: The foundation opens a sexual-assault trauma recovery center (展心性侵害創傷復原中心) to support long-term healing after the immediate crisis ends.

timeline.label: 'Only YES means YES' campaign
timeline.detail: On the eve of its 30th anniversary, Modern Women's Foundation launches its 'only YES means YES — without consent, it is sexual assault' (沒有同意，就是性侵) public education campaign, which it has repeated with a new theme every year since.

timeline.label: Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act
timeline.detail: Modern Women's Foundation has pushed for a stalking law since 2013 and sent its own draft to the legislature in 2015. After a high-profile case in 2021, Taiwan passes the Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act in November 2021. It takes effect in June 2022, criminalizing repeated sex- or gender-related stalking and harassment.

sections.title: Before the laws: when police refused to take reports

blocks.text: In 1987, when Modern Women's Foundation was established in May, Taiwan was still under martial law, which would not be lifted until 15 July of that year. Women had gained the right to vote decades earlier, but the legal system offered almost no protection against violence inside the home or in intimate relationships. A husband beating a wife was considered a family matter. A woman reporting sexual assault faced police who might refuse to take her statement, doctors who might refuse to treat her, and a legal code that classified rape as an offense against public morality rather than against her person.

The foundation's English-language history describes what victims faced: 'police did not accept their cases, medical professionals refused to treat them, and there were no other governmental services provided to assist them.' The Chinese version of the same history adds that social-welfare offices offered no help either, so victims who had nowhere else to go turned to the foundation. A later Taipei Times retrospective, citing a report by the Foundation of Women's Rights Promotion and Development, describes the same period: a man beating a woman on the street could justify it to bystanders by saying 'she is my wife', and people assumed she must have done something wrong to deserve it.

This was the gap Modern Women's Foundation set out to fill: not only advocacy and law reform, which groups like Awakening Foundation were already doing, but direct services to women whose safety was in immediate danger and who had nowhere else to turn.

sections.title: 1987 to 1988: from general rights to urgent protection

blocks.text: Pan Wei-kang (潘維剛), then a member of the Taipei City Council (she served there from 25 December 1981 to 31 January 1993), founded Modern Women's Foundation in 1987 with a group of people committed to women's rights. The foundation's original purpose, according to its own account, was to help women navigate the balance between traditional and modern roles. But as soon as they began working, they discovered that many women could not even think about balancing roles because they were not safe.

In 1988 the foundation opened the Women's Guardian Center (婦女護衛中心), Taiwan's first center dedicated to protecting women and children from sexual assault, domestic violence and sexual harassment. The center brought together lawyers, crime-prevention experts, doctors and social workers to provide what the state would not: legal advice, accompaniment to medical appointments and police interviews, and other emergency services. It was the first organization in Taiwan to do this work, and it had to invent the model as it went.

Pan Wei-kang's own political career gave the foundation unusual leverage. She served as a legislator from 1993 to 2002 and again from 2005 to 2016 for the Kuomintang. That let her draft bills, lobby colleagues and push for passage from inside the legislature. The combination of direct service and legislative power is rare. Most organizations do one or the other. Modern Women's Foundation did both.

sections.kicker: The cases that changed the law
sections.title: Deng Ru-wen and Peng Wan-ru: two tragedies that made reform urgent

blocks.text: Two events in the 1990s turned the Women's Guardian Center's quiet case-by-case work into a national legislative campaign.

The first was the 1993 case of Deng Ru-wen (鄧如雯). Lin A-chi, a man twenty-two years older with a prior conviction for taking part in a killing, raped Deng when she was a teenager. She became pregnant, gave birth and was pushed into living with him, and he beat her for years. When she ran home, he smashed her parents' belongings, tied up her father and threatened her family. On the night of 27 October 1993, after he came home drunk and threatened to kill her family again, Deng killed Lin after he had gone to sleep. She then turned herself in.

Deng's trial became a referendum on how Taiwan treated domestic violence. Women's groups, including Awakening Foundation, rallied to her defense. Her defence, which included lawyer Wang Ju-hsuan (王如玄), argued that prolonged abuse had left her in a state of mental exhaustion. The Banqiao District Court sentenced her to five years and six months. In August 1994 the Taiwan High Court, citing her voluntary surrender and her impaired mental state, reduced the sentence to three years. She was paroled in March 1996, after less than a year in prison.

The case exposed the absence of any legal framework for domestic violence. Deng had tried to leave, had reported to police, and had been forced back by Lin's escalating violence. The system had no tools to protect her except after she had already killed her abuser. In February 1994, the day before Deng's first verdict, Awakening Foundation and other women's groups visited Justice Minister Ma Ying-jeou to ask for a law against marital violence. He promised training for judicial staff and administrative rules, but not yet a law. According to the Taipei Times, citing Lin Chih-li's study of how the act was made, the Ministry of the Interior then gave NT$1 million for research on a draft, but the effort stalled after the first report for lack of staff and further funding.

The second event was the murder of Peng Wan-ru (彭婉如) on 30 November 1996. Peng was the director of the Democratic Progressive Party's Women's Affairs Department and a well-known feminist. She disappeared in Kaohsiung the night before a DPP convention after getting into a taxi. Her body was later found outside an abandoned warehouse in Kaohsiung County with more than thirty stab wounds. She had been raped. The murder was never solved.

Peng's death produced nationwide outrage. Ironically, the DPP convention she had been attending passed her proposal to reserve one-quarter of party seats for women on the day she is believed to have been killed. Women's groups organized a massive march in December 1996. The domestic violence effort restarted when Pan Wei-kang learned that judge Kao Feng-hsian (高鳳仙) had already written a draft based on laws in the United States and New Zealand, covering family violence in general rather than only violence between spouses. That bill went to the legislature in July 1996, months before Peng's death. According to the foundation, Peng's murder pushed the Executive Yuan to take women's personal safety seriously and sped up passage of the sexual assault bill the foundation had already commissioned. The foundation's own account says it set up a committee in 1996 to build a domestic violence law suited to Taiwan, with Kao as drafter and with experts, NGOs, government agencies and survivors involved, and that Pan then worked with legislators from several parties to pass it. On 21 December 1996 women marched at night in Taipei under the slogan 'Women want rights, not violence' (女人要權力，不要暴力). The Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act passed soon after, and the domestic violence law followed about eighteen months later.

sections.title: Four laws in eight years: the legislative record

blocks.text: Modern Women's Foundation co-drafted or drafted four major laws between 1997 and 2005. Each one filled a gap the earlier system had left open.

The Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act passed in January 1997. The foundation commissioned Liao Shu-wen (廖書雯) to draft the bill, and it became the first law pushed through jointly by women legislators of the KMT, DPP and New Party, including Pan Wei-kang, Yeh Chu-lan and Chu Hui-liang. The foundation calls it Taiwan's first law to protect the personal safety of women and children. It established sexual assault prevention centers in every city and county, required coordination among police, medical, social-service and education agencies, mandated prevention education in schools, set up a national offender registry, and created victim services including accompaniment, counseling and legal aid. Before this law, sexual assault victims had nowhere to go for coordinated help. After it, every local government had to provide a center.

The Domestic Violence Prevention Act passed on 24 June 1998 and took effect in 1999. Taiwan became Asia's first country to have a civil protection order system for domestic violence. The act defined domestic violence broadly, covering physical, psychological and economic abuse between family members, spouses and cohabitants. It allowed courts to issue emergency, temporary and long-term protection orders that could bar an abuser from the home, require them to stay a set distance away, and mandate counseling or treatment. It also created family-violence service centers and a mandatory reporting system. Judge Kao Feng-hsian drafted it for the committee Modern Women's Foundation set up in 1996.

The Criminal Code amendment of 1999, pushed through the legislature by Pan Wei-kang, restructured how Taiwan's legal system understood rape. Before 1999, sexual offenses sat in a chapter called 'offenses against morality' (妨害風化), which treated rape as a public-decency crime rather than a violation of a person's autonomy. The amendment created a new chapter, 'offenses against sexual autonomy' (妨害性自主), and made clear that forced sex was a crime against the victim's will, not against society's sense of propriety. The reform also changed rape from a complaint-only offense to a public offense and explicitly recognized that a husband could rape his wife, which earlier interpretations had left unclear.

The Sexual Harassment Prevention Act of 2005 was the last of the four. The Gender Equality in Employment Act and the Gender Equity Education Act already covered harassment at work and in schools, but public spaces had no protection. Modern Women's Foundation proposed a bill to close that gap. The Sexual Harassment Prevention Act passed in early 2005 and took effect in February 2006, covering harassment in any setting not addressed by the other two laws and setting up complaint and investigation procedures.

After 2005, the foundation continued to push for amendments. In 2015 it worked with a team of lawyers to reform the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act again, adding protections for child victims in court, establishing expert witnesses for child and disability cases, and banning anyone from sharing information that could identify a victim. The foundation began pushing for a stalking law in 2013, convened a working group that finished a draft Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act in 2015, and adapted Dr. TK Logan's stalking risk-assessment tool (SHARP) for Taiwan. After a high-profile case in 2021, the act passed its third reading in November 2021 and took effect on 1 June 2022.

sections.title: What a protection center does: from hotlines to court social workers

blocks.text: The foundation's English introduction says it assists more than 8,000 victims of domestic violence, sexual assault and sexual harassment each year, and also helps nearly 3,000 high-conflict families in the courts each year. Those are large numbers, close to Garden of Hope's scale in some areas, and they reflect a service model built around crisis response and legal accompaniment rather than long-term residential care.

The core services include twenty-four-hour hotlines, emergency shelter referrals, hospital and police accompaniment, legal advice, court support and counseling. In 2002 Modern Women's Foundation established Taiwan's first family-violence service center inside Shilin District Court in Taipei. Social workers stationed at the court help victims file protection orders, understand legal procedures, access welfare resources and find safe housing. The foundation notes that the model is now used nationwide. From 2013 it also began running family-case service centers (家事服務中心) in district courts such as Taichung and Taipei, for parties in divorce and custody cases.

The foundation also runs programs for populations that face extra barriers: intimate-partner violence among LGBTQ couples, which it began addressing in 2009 in partnership with the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association; and dating violence among teenagers, which it has worked on since 2008 with more than sixty school talks a year. In 2016 it launched the 'Love Is Respect' programme and set up 戀愛乾麻醬, which it describes as Taiwan's first website for helping young people practise healthy relationships.

In 2017 the foundation opened a sexual-assault trauma recovery center (展心性侵害創傷復原中心) to provide longer-term support after the crisis phase. That same year it expanded services in Hualien and Hsinchu to include children who witness domestic violence, recognizing that those children are also victims even if they are not directly harmed.

This is a different model from Garden of Hope's network of shelters and long-term residential programs, and different again from Awakening Foundation's law-reform and hotline work. Modern Women's Foundation sits in between: it provides direct crisis services, but the services are built to get people through the legal and medical systems rather than to house them for months. It also continues to draft and lobby for laws, but its main identity is as a protection center, not a policy think tank.

sections.title: How Taiwan's laws require foundations to report

blocks.text: Two laws govern how Taiwan's foundations and charities must disclose their finances and activities: the Foundations Act of 2018 (財團法人法) and the Charity Fundraising Act (公益勸募條例).

The Foundations Act requires every foundation to submit its annual work plan and budget to the supervising authority within one month of the start of the year, and its work report and financial statements within five months of year-end. Foundations above a certain size must have their financial statements audited by a certified public accountant. Those documents must then be publicly disclosed within one month after they are filed with the authority for the record. Foundations must also disclose a list of donors and recipients from the previous year, including names and amounts, unless a donor or recipient objects in writing in advance, or disclosure would hinder or seriously affect operations, and the competent authority agrees. Disclosure can be by newspaper, website or public inspection. Under Article 29, directors or supervisors who falsify records or fail to file the required reports can be fined NT$30,000 to NT$150,000.

The Charity Fundraising Act applies to specific fundraising campaigns rather than to general operations. Any organization that conducts a public fundraising drive must report the campaign results to the supervising authority within thirty days after the campaign period ends, including a list of donors, total funds raised and an income-and-expenditure report. The organization must also publicly disclose that information. Separately, when the funds are spent, the organization must file a completion report within thirty days after the use plan is completed, showing how the money was used, with outcome data and receipts. The deadline for the completion report can be extended by up to thirty days if needed. Article 20 also requires these reports to be posted on the supervising authority's website, so anyone can look up a permitted campaign and see how its money was used. Article 18 adds that any spending of NT$10,000 or more from campaign funds must be paid by cheque or bank or postal transfer, not in cash.

Modern Women's Foundation lists annual reports and financial audit reports on its website under a section called '財務簽證報告' (audited financial reports). The reports are organized by year, with the most recent covering 2025 (民國114年). The foundation's legal name is 財團法人現代婦女教育基金會, and its tax ID is 76904597. The foundation explains that its 2015 (民國104年) report was a combined statement for two foundations that share an office but keep separate finances: the national 財團法人現代婦女教育基金會 and the Taipei-focused 財團法人台北市現代婦女基金會. The website footer also lists two current Ministry of Health and Welfare fundraising permit numbers (勸募字號), and its social accountability (社會責信) section has monthly donor lists, a personal donation lookup and reports on each permitted fundraising campaign (勸募方案徵信).

Because I did not check the audited statements line by line, this lesson cannot provide specific income, spending or reserve figures the way the Awakening Foundation lesson did. What it can say is that the law requires those figures to exist, to be audited and to be published. A potential partner such as cool dairy should ask for the most recent audited financial statement, the breakdown of income by source, the ratio of program spending to administrative overhead, and an explanation of any large changes from year to year.

sections.title: How a shop could partner transparently

blocks.text: If cool dairy wants to donate proceeds to Modern Women's Foundation, there are several standard models used by Taiwan shops and brands.

The foundation already has public channels for this kind of cooperation. Its website has a corporate participation page (企業參與), a 'you shop, they donate' page (你購物他捐款) listing brands that give part of their sales, and a charity merchandise page (義賣商品). Reading those pages first will show cool dairy what formats the foundation already accepts and how it credits partners.

items: Percentage of sales: the shop commits to donating a fixed percentage of revenue from all sales, or from a specific product line, during a set period. Example: 'Five percent of every purchase in November 2026 goes to Modern Women's Foundation.' This model requires the shop to keep clear sales records and issue a single donation at the end of the period.

Lump-sum donation with storytelling: the shop donates a fixed amount up front and tells customers that their purchases supported that donation. Example: 'cool dairy donated NT$50,000 to Modern Women's Foundation this quarter. Your support made that possible.' This is simpler to execute and report, and it avoids the complexity of tying individual transactions to charity.

Product-specific partnership: the shop sells a co-branded item or a limited-edition piece and donates all or part of the profit. Example: a tote bag designed with the foundation's input, where the proceeds after costs go to the organization. This works well for items that can carry a message or tell a story.

Invoice donation code: Taiwan's electronic invoice system lets customers donate their receipt's lottery chance to a registered charity by entering a 'love code' (愛心碼). The shop can print the foundation's code on receipts or packaging. The foundation's website would list its code, or cool dairy can ask for it. This is a zero-cost way to let customers give directly without requiring the shop to collect and forward money.

blocks.text: Whichever model cool dairy chooses, transparency means documenting the partnership in writing, keeping receipts, getting a donation receipt from the foundation, and publishing the total donated and when. Under the Charity Fundraising Act, if the shop's campaign counts as public fundraising—meaning it publicly solicits money tied to a cause—cool dairy would need to apply for a permit and file reports. However, only public schools, administrative legal persons, public-interest associations, and foundations may obtain fundraising permits under the Act; a for-profit shop cannot. If cool dairy wants to publicly solicit donations, it must do so under Modern Women's Foundation's own permitted campaign. If the shop is simply donating its own revenue and telling customers about it afterward, that is not public fundraising and requires no permit. The distinction matters. Before launching, cool dairy should confirm with the foundation and, if needed, a lawyer which model applies.

Modern Women's Foundation, like other established organizations, likely has standard partnership agreements and knows which models require permits. The first step is to ask. The second step is to be clear with customers: tell them exactly how much will be donated, when, to whom, and for what. The third step is to follow through and report the outcome.

sections.title: Modern Women's Foundation, Garden of Hope and Awakening: three models

blocks.text: The three organizations covered so far in this series—Awakening Foundation, Garden of Hope Foundation and Modern Women's Foundation—represent three different approaches to women's rights work, and understanding the differences helps clarify what a donation supports.

There is also a comparison beyond Taiwan. According to the Taipei Times, judge Kao Feng-hsian, who drafted the bill for Modern Women's Foundation's committee, went on to help Japan draft its own domestic violence law, which Japan adopted in 2001. Taiwan's 1998 act was therefore not only Asia's first; it also became a reference point for a neighbour.

Awakening Foundation is mainly an advocacy and watchdog organization. Its total income in 2025 was about NT$5.7 million. It has six or seven paid staff. Its products are draft bills, policy reports, lobby campaigns, volunteer trainings and public pressure. It does run a family-law advice hotline, but most of its work is aimed at changing systems rather than helping individuals through them.

Garden of Hope Foundation is mainly a service provider, and a large one. Its total income in 2025 was about NT$640.7 million. It runs shelters, halfway houses, employment programs and counseling centers across Taiwan, many under government contracts. It also advocates for laws and policies, but its identity is as an organization that operates facilities and delivers long-term case management. Its scale is more than a hundred times Awakening's.

Modern Women's Foundation is both: it provides crisis services to thousands of victims each year, and it drafts laws. Its own figures, more than 8,000 victims and nearly 3,000 court families a year, show a large service operation. I have not compared its income with Garden of Hope's, so check the audited reports before drawing conclusions about size. It also retains the legislative access that Pan Wei-kang brought when she founded it, even though she is no longer in the legislature. This dual identity—service provider and lawmaker—is unusual.

For a shop like cool dairy, the choice among them is not about which is better but about what story the shop wants to tell. Supporting Awakening means supporting the people who write the laws. Supporting Garden of Hope means supporting shelters and long-term care. Supporting Modern Women's Foundation means supporting the organizations that stand between a victim and the police station, the hospital and the courthouse, at the moment of crisis, and that also built the legal tools those institutions now use.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Modern Women's Foundation helped draft the laws that created Taiwan's domestic violence protection system, and it pioneered court service centers that it still operates today. Should a donor give to the organization that built the legal framework, even if the government now enforces those laws and runs national hotlines? Or should the donor only support work the organization still directly controls, like the court centers and crisis services it continues to provide?

fun_fact.title: A plush bear that does the fundraising
fun_fact.text: Modern Women's Foundation says domestic violence was hard to explain to the public and hard to raise money for, because the subject is dark and people turn away from it. Around 2020 it created its own character brand, Hu Hu Universe (呼呼小宇宙): a guardian plush toy meant to stand for comfort and companionship after trauma. The foundation licenses Hu Hu for co-branded products, and in 2021 it sent the character on a touring exhibition through department stores and office lobbies in greater Taipei. A year later it contributed a piece to the 'Perfect Victim' (完美受害人) exhibition, which used the clothes survivors had been wearing to challenge the idea that what a woman wears explains an assault. Both projects are worth knowing for cool dairy: one shows a charity using merchandise and design to fund hard work, and the other shows clothing itself being used as evidence against victim blaming.

Taiwan's law covering sexual harassment outside the workplace and school settings, passed in 2005 and in force from February 2006. Proposed by Modern Women's Foundation.
Taiwan's 2021 law criminalizing repeated sex- or gender-related stalking and harassment. It took effect in June 2022.
Taiwan's national 24-hour hotline for domestic violence, sexual assault and child protection, established in 2001 by consolidating earlier local hotlines.
A court order in Taiwan that can bar a domestic violence offender from the home, require them to stay away, and mandate treatment. Introduced by the 1998 Domestic Violence Prevention Act.
The 1999 reframing of sexual assault crimes in Taiwan's Criminal Code, replacing the older 'offenses against morality' chapter and treating rape as a violation of the victim's autonomy.
The old Criminal Code chapter under which sexual offenses were classified before 1999, treating rape as a crime against public decency rather than personal rights.
Taiwan's 2018 law governing foundations, requiring them to file annual work plans, budgets, reports and audited financial statements, and to disclose them publicly.

Taiwan's law requiring organizations that conduct public fundraising to report donors, amounts and proceeds within thirty days after the campaign period ends, and to file a completion report with outcomes within thirty days after the use plan is completed.
A code Taiwan shoppers can enter at checkout to donate their electronic invoice's lottery chance to a registered charity.

A service center inside a courthouse where social workers help domestic violence victims file protection orders, access legal advice and connect to resources. Modern Women's Foundation pioneered this model in 2002.

aliases: 展心性侵害創傷復原中心
glossary.explain: A center opened by Modern Women's Foundation in 2017 to provide long-term support for sexual assault survivors after the immediate crisis phase.
A website launched by Modern Women's Foundation in 2016, under its 'Love Is Respect' programme, to help young people learn about healthy relationships and prevent dating violence.

aliases: 台灣同志諮詢熱線協會
glossary.explain: An LGBTQ advocacy and support organization in Taiwan. It partnered with Modern Women's Foundation in 2009 to address intimate-partner violence in same-sex couples.
A district court in Taipei where Modern Women's Foundation opened Taiwan's first court-based family-violence service center in 2002.
Huiru's planned vintage shop whose proceeds are meant to support Taiwan women's organizations. The setting for this lesson's partnership discussion.
The emergency rule in force in Taiwan from 1949 to July 1987, which restricted civil liberties and banned opposition parties.
Taiwan's Minister of Justice when women's groups asked him in February 1994 for a law against marital violence; later President of Taiwan (2008–2016).
One of Taiwan's two major political parties, generally associated with Taiwan independence and progressive social policies. Peng Wan-ru worked for its Women's Affairs Department.
One of Taiwan's two major political parties, historically associated with reunification with China. Pan Wei-kang served as a KMT legislator.
A feminist advocacy foundation founded in 1982 as a magazine and registered as a foundation in 1987. Focused on law reform, policy and a family-law hotline.
A large Christian-rooted foundation founded in 1988 that runs shelters, counseling and job training for victims of gender-based violence.
An organization that provides direct crisis services to victims of violence, such as hotlines, emergency shelter referrals, hospital accompaniment and legal support.
An organization whose main work is changing laws, policies and public opinion rather than providing direct services to individuals.
A foundation in Taiwan: a legal body built around a fund of property and run by a board, governed by the Foundations Act.
A fundraising campaign that publicly solicits donations tied to a charitable cause. In Taiwan, such campaigns often require a government permit and must file detailed reports.
A receipt issued by a registered charity in Taiwan to document a donation, often needed for tax deductions or to prove compliance with fundraising laws.
A financial statement reviewed and certified by an independent accountant. Taiwan law requires foundations above a certain size to have their statements audited.

A guardian plush-toy character brand (IP) Modern Women's Foundation created around 2020 because domestic violence was hard to explain and hard to raise money for. It is licensed for co-branded products.
Modern Women's Foundation's affirmative-consent campaign, launched in 2017 and renewed with a new theme each year.
A professor who helped build Taiwan's domestic violence safety network in 2007 and joined the 2015 sexual assault law reform team.
A lawyer and Modern Women's Foundation board member who led and wrote the 2015 amendment of the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act.

aliases: Stalking and Harassment Assessment and Risk Profile
glossary.explain: A stalking risk-assessment tool developed by Dr. TK Logan, which Modern Women's Foundation adapted for Taiwan in 2015.

aliases: 完美受害人―性侵衣物展
glossary.explain: A 2022 exhibition organised by the KAOS team that told stories of sexual violence through the clothes survivors wore; Modern Women's Foundation contributed a work.
An alliance of NGOs that grew out of the 2001 Domestic Violence Prevention Law Amendment League, which Modern Women's Foundation helped start. Judge Kao Feng-hsian was its founding chair.
Author of a study of how Taiwan's Domestic Violence Prevention Act was made, cited by the Taipei Times for the early history of the bill.
The slogan of the night march in Taipei on 21 December 1996, after Peng Wan-ru's murder, demanding women's right to walk safely after dark.
